source_title: Restrictions on Use of Unmanned Aircraft Systems — Definition — Violation — Cause of Action and Damages
regulated_activity: UAS surveillance/recording of targeted persons or private property without consent
requirement_type: Civil prohibition (private right of action, not criminal)
summary: §21-213(2)(a) prohibits using a UAS to intentionally surveil, gather evidence about, or record specifically targeted persons or specifically targeted private property (dwelling/curtilage or farm/ranch/commercial/industrial property) without written consent. §21-213(1)(b)(ii) excludes from the statute's 'unmanned aircraft system' definition any UAS 'used in mapping or resource management,' removing mapping/survey-purpose flights from the consent requirement. §21-213(4) permits a facility owner/easement holder to aerially inspect their own facilities on land owned by another. Enforcement is civil: greater of $1,000 or actual damages, plus attorney's fees.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Because the mapping/resource-management exclusion is purpose-based, log the survey/mapping purpose of each flight at planning time rather than after the fact — that record is what lets you rely on the exclusion instead of the consent requirement. The easement-inspection exemption directly supports utility/infrastructure inspection performed under a right of occupancy, so keep a copy of the easement or access agreement in the project file.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This carve-out is a defense to a civil claim, not immunity from being sued — a property owner can still bring an action and force you to establish that the flight was genuinely for mapping/resource management. Keep contemporaneous flight logs, mission plans, and deliverable descriptions tied to each flight so the mapping purpose is documented before any dispute arises, not reconstructed afterward.

issuing_authority: Idaho Legislature / Idaho Department of Correction
source_title: Unmanned aircraft — restricted airspace over correctional facilities
regulated_activity: Operating a drone within restricted airspace of an IDOC facility (surface to 400 ft AGL within facility perimeter)
summary: Signed March 31, 2026, effective July 1, 2026. Makes it unlawful to operate a UAS within the 'restricted airspace' of an Idaho Department of Correction facility, defined as surface to 400 ft AGL within the facility's fenced/posted perimeter. Misdemeanor: up to $1,000 fine, up to 6 months county jail, and/or drone forfeiture. Authorizes IDOC and law enforcement to take mitigation measures (e.g., jamming) against a drone operating in a 'nefarious manner' in that airspace. Lack of knowledge that the area is a correctional facility is not a defense.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Map the facility perimeter and 400 ft AGL ceiling into your pre-flight planning tool before any job near an Idaho correctional facility, and treat active jamming as a real operational risk to project equipment — not just a legal abstraction — since the statute authorizes it against drones operating in the restricted airspace.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This is a brand-new statute (effective mid-2026) that most third-party drone-law summaries won't yet reflect, so don't rely on older secondary sources. Obtain written IDOC coordination before any flight near a correctional facility; the 'lack of knowledge is not a defense' provision means good-faith ignorance of a facility boundary will not protect the operator or the firm.

issuing_authority: Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation
regulated_party: UAS operators in Idaho state parks
regulated_activity: Drone operation in a state park
summary: Drone operation in an Idaho state park may be authorized by the park or program manager when it does not interfere with traditional park uses and is consistent with resource preservation. Not a blanket ban, but not open by default.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Contact the specific park manager early in project scheduling — this is a discretionary, per-park approval, not a standard permit form, so lead time can vary widely by park.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Start with the site manager or permitting office for Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation before scheduling fieldwork, because property-specific conditions may control the route and timing. Request the current form, lead time, fee, insurance and FAA-document checklist, and site restrictions, then keep the signed approval and conditions in the mission file.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Get the park manager's authorization in writing (email is sufficient) and keep it in the project file; a verbal go-ahead is not a reliable compliance record.

source_title: Public Use of Lands Owned or Controlled by Idaho Fish and Game
regulated_activity: Landing or launching aircraft (rule's 'Aircraft' definition expressly includes 'any unmanned aircraft system')
permit_or_approval_required: Yes - Commission, Director, Regional Supervisor, or designee authorization
summary: IDAPA 13.01.03.010.1 defines 'Aircraft' to expressly include 'any unmanned aircraft system.' Rule 100.01.20 prohibits landing or launching aircraft on Department of Fish and Game lands/water except on public airstrips, unless specifically authorized by the Commission, Director, Regional Supervisor, or designee.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat any WMA or IDFG access site the same as a state park for launch/landing purposes — get prior authorization before staging a crew there for environmental monitoring or habitat-mapping work. Flying over WMA land from an off-site launch point avoids this specific rule but should still respect wildlife-harassment concerns.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Contact Idaho Fish and Game Commission before fixing the mobilization date and ask for the current application or approval route, supporting-document checklist, fees, and processing estimate. Describe the proposed site, dates, purpose, aircraft, operator, and requested exception clearly, and retain the issued approval and all conditions; the captured requirement is: Yes - Commission, Director, Regional Supervisor, or designee authorization.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Because 'aircraft' is expressly defined to include UAS, do not treat this as a gray area — obtain and retain written IDFG authorization before any launch/landing on Department land, the same way you would for a state park permit.
